title: The raggedy bus and the man with the rifle
summary: Dance mentions Hines's "Freedom Riders"; Ramirez recounts a road crew roadblock stand-off with a rifle-wielding man while the white driver maneuvered the bus.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I guess the fact that the bands were touring all

through...you know, one after another, more or less... It must have been... You know, Earl Hines always referred to... He said, "We were the first Freedom Riders." And it must have had a very good effect, you know, no matter what...

Well, I don't know about Freedom Riders. We had this bus. It was a raggedy-looking bus. It wasn't a bad... It was a little lopsided. But unfortunately, we had a very... Always you would have a sympathetic White driver with the band! This guy was sitting on the road with a rifle cocked, and he says, "I'm not going to move. You move that bus around." Well, of course, the guy had to figure out a way to go inside of a mountain at an angle of 45 degrees or so...
Who told him to move the bus around?
Well, this character with his legs crossed in the middle of the road. Now, they were fixing the road.

They're fixing the road, and he's sitting on the side where the barricade is. All he has to do is just move a little, and the bus will go around. He says he's not going. You've got the mountain on the wrong side. When he saw the people that were in there, I guess he ...(?)... So things like that.
